4df862c5af:
This chapter starts with what a CLAUDE.md file physically is. Then it covers how Claude Code finds and loads the memory files that apply to a session, what each level of the hierarchy is for, and who can see it.

You'll see how @import and .claude/rules/ keep memory modular, and how rules with paths frontmatter load only when matching files are touched. And you'll learn to diagnose the commonest failure: the instruction that works for you and not for your teammate.

The story runs from dotfile and Maven/Spring configuration cascades to a measured split of a 592-line file. Python and Java/Spring comparisons run throughout.
07de642107:
Reading time: 2.5 to 3 hours  ·  Companion code, 16 Python examples, 2 Java programs and a set of repo fixtures for this chapter: ccarf-companion/08-claude-md-rules/ (run bash run_all.sh; everything works offline, and none of this chapter's examples calls the model).

Chapter 07 covers the same project-versus-user scoping for MCP servers (.mcp.json in git, personal servers outside it). It also covers the built-in Read, Write and Edit tools, which trigger on-demand memory loading here. Chapter 09 covers Skills and slash commands, the on-demand alternative to memory for procedures.
50f410bd14:
A CLAUDE.md file is ordinary Markdown that Claude Code finds by its location, reads from disk and places into the model's context window as text, so the location of a file decides who receives its instructions and when, and every token in it is paid for on every request after it loads.

Because memory is text and not configuration, the design job is to put each instruction at the narrowest location that still reaches everyone who needs it (user, project, directory, or a rule scoped by file pattern), to keep what always loads short, to load the rest only when the files it concerns are touched, and to move anything that must be guaranteed out of memory and into permissions or hooks.
8a89d10e11:
The official task statement for 3.1 lists the knowledge you need:

  • the hierarchy: user-level, project-level and directory-level;
  • user-level settings apply only to that user and are not shared through version control;
  • the @import syntax for referencing external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular;
  • the .claude/rules/ directory as an alternative to a single large file.

The skills it names are these. Diagnose a hierarchy problem, such as a teammate not receiving instructions that live in a user-level file. Use @import to include relevant standards selectively. Split a large CLAUDE.md into focused rule files. And use the /memory command to verify which memory files are loaded.

Task statement 3.3 adds the other half of modularity. Rule files can carry YAML frontmatter with a paths field of glob patterns, and they load only when Claude edits matching files. For conventions that cut across directories, this beats directory-level CLAUDE.md files.

The official sample question is about test files spread throughout a codebase, each next to the code it tests. The team wants one set of testing conventions applied wherever a test file is created.
30d5d67381:
Every exam question in this area comes down to one of three consequences of "memory is text chosen by location".

Location is scope. A rule written in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md exists on one machine. A rule in the repository root reaches every clone. A rule in services/billing/CLAUDE.md reaches sessions that touch billing.

Loaded text costs tokens. A bloated file is slower, more expensive and less reliably followed than a short one. Splitting it only helps if the pieces load conditionally.

Memory is guidance. It changes what the model is likely to do, and it prevents nothing. So "never do X" belongs in permissions or a hook.

The rest of the chapter makes each of these concrete, with a loading algorithm, a measured token budget, and runnable simulations.
eb6591b569:
A Java reader should carry one analogy and one disanalogy into the chapter.

The analogy: the hierarchy is externalized configuration. Spring has application.yml in the jar, application-prod.yml for a profile, and environment variables and command-line arguments on top. Maven has a parent POM, the project POM, and ~/.m2/settings.xml. Each is a layered mechanism where the file's location says who it applies to.

The disanalogy is the one this chapter keeps coming back to. Spring resolves each property to one value by precedence, and Maven's child POM overrides the parent's. Claude Code concatenates. Every applicable memory file ends up in the context as text. When two of them disagree, the model reads both and decides. Nothing is overridden, so nothing can be relied on to win.
0185fe673a: Layered, location-based configuration is one of the oldest ideas in tooling. CLAUDE.md is a recent member of a long family. Tracing that family explains why the design looks the way it does, and where the new member differs from the old ones.
9dc068eca7:
Unix settled the first pattern. A shell reads /etc/profile for the machine, then ~/.profile or ~/.bashrc for the user. Editors, mail clients and compilers followed with the same two-level convention. There's a system-wide default under /etc and a personal override under the home directory, both in plain text a human can open. Names starting with a dot are hidden from directory listings, which is where the word dotfile comes from.

Two properties of this design matter here. First, the user file is personal and unversioned: it follows the person, not the project. Second, the later file wins. The shell runs the files in order, and a later assignment replaces an earlier one.

In configuration languages that assign variables, "last one wins" is automatic. In text read by a language model, it isn't.
ae301d5519:
The weak spot of the two-level scheme was the missing middle. A project that wanted its own conventions had no standard place to put them. So teams wrote them in a README that tools couldn't read, or in a wiki nobody opened.

Personal dotfiles tried to fill the gap with per-directory hacks. The result was a familiar story: one developer's shell producing different results from another's on the same checkout.
6dac358c45:
Source control gave the middle layer a home: files that live in the repository and travel with a clone.

  • Git (2005) made the pattern famous with .gitignore. It can appear in any directory and applies to that subtree. Rules from deeper files take precedence over rules from shallower ones, and a negation syntax re-includes what a parent excluded.
  • Maven 2 (2005) put pom.xml in every module. A module can name a <parent> and inherit its dependency management and plugin configuration. The per-user ~/.m2/settings.xml holds what must not be committed, such as credentials and mirror URLs.
  • EditorConfig (around 2011) gave editors a single .editorconfig. The tool finds it by walking up the directory tree and stops at a file containing root = true. The nearest file wins per key. ESLint's cascading .eslintrc files worked the same way.
  • Spring Boot (2014) externalized configuration into a documented precedence list: command-line arguments over environment variables over profile-specific files over the packaged application.yml.
46b0ab3534:
All of these are resolvers. Given a key, they return exactly one value, chosen by a rule. That's what makes them predictable. It's also what CLAUDE.md does not do.

What CLAUDE.md inherits from this family is the structure. There's a managed level for the organization, and a user level that is personal and not in version control. There's a project level in the repository, plus directory levels that apply to a subtree, discovered by walking the directory tree.

Companion example 02_lineage_cascades.py runs all of these on the same layered inputs: a gitignore-style cascade, an EditorConfig walk with root = true, and a Spring property resolver beside a CLAUDE.md concatenation. One run makes the contrast visible. If you'd rather read it in Java, java/ConfigPrecedence.java does the same for a Spring-style resolver.
aa27a8226e:
Coding assistants brought the next step. Tools that put a language model in the editor needed a place for "how this team writes code". Several arrived at the same answer within a year or two: a Markdown or plain text file in the repository that the tool reads and adds to the prompt. Examples include Cursor's .cursorrules (and later its .cursor/rules directory with per-rule glob patterns), GitHub Copilot's .github/copilot-instructions.md, and the cross-tool AGENTS.md convention.

Claude Code's CLAUDE.md belongs to this family and reads like it: plain text, committed, one file per scope. The current docs also let Claude Code read an AGENTS.md when a repository has no CLAUDE.md. And /init can fold other tools' rule files into a starter CLAUDE.md.

Two ideas from the older family were kept, and one was added. Kept: the scope hierarchy, and the personal, unversioned layer. Added: rules that load by file pattern (the path-specific rules of task statement 3.3). These have no real ancestor in the dotfile world. A shell doesn't care which file you're editing. A language model does.
78a0f019ac:
The deepest difference is the reader. A shell or a build tool parses a file and gets a deterministic result. A conflict is resolved by a rule, and a typo is a loud error.

A language model reads the text, weighs it against everything else in the context, and produces a probable continuation. A vague sentence isn't an error; it's a weak signal. A contradiction isn't resolved; it's a coin flip with a bias. A forgotten instruction costs nothing at load time, then shows up three hours later as behaviour you didn't want.

Every practice in this chapter (short files, specific wording, scoped loading, enforcement elsewhere) is a way of making a probabilistic reader behave predictably.
ce4a45ed09:
Claude Code starts every session with a fresh context window. Nothing from yesterday's conversation is there. What carries over is what's on disk, and CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for writing down what you'd otherwise re-explain.

At session start, Claude Code finds the memory files that apply (the next sections give the algorithm), reads them, and includes their text in the first request to the model.

The docs state a detail that's easy to miss and useful in practice. The content arrives as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of the system prompt itself. The model reads it the way it reads any other input from you. It tries to follow it. There's no guarantee of strict compliance, especially for vague or conflicting instructions.
60a379b440:
Three consequences follow from the file being text in the context.

First, there is no schema. Claude Code doesn't parse CLAUDE.md into settings. A line that says "run pnpm test before committing" isn't a hook that runs a command. It's a sentence that the model, which has a Bash tool, will usually act on. Claude Code itself interprets only the structures it needs to load files: the @path import syntax, the paths frontmatter in rule files, and block-level HTML comments. It strips those comments, so you can leave notes for maintainers without paying tokens for them (comments inside code blocks are preserved).

Second, the cost is real and recurring. The text rides along in the input of every request in the session. The prompt cache can make repeated input cheaper (check the docs for current pricing multipliers). But cached tokens still occupy the window, and they still compete with your actual task for the model's attention.

Third, position and neighbours matter. The model weighs a rule differently when it's one of fifteen lines than when it's one of nine hundred. It also weighs it differently when the file ends with the rule than when the rule is buried between two unrelated ones.
372ddfe4b2:
The token numbers make the cost tangible. The Claude Code docs include an interactive walkthrough of a context window with representative figures:

  • roughly 4,200 tokens of system prompt;
  • a few hundred for the environment block;
  • about 320 for a short user CLAUDE.md;
  • about 1,800 for a project CLAUDE.md;
  • 290 to 380 for a path-scoped rule when it loads.

The docs call these illustrative. The point is the shape. Memory is a modest, fixed slice at the front of the window. A file of 9,000 tokens would be larger than everything else in that startup block combined.

Chapter 07 listed the built-in tools whose results (file reads, search output) land in the same window. Memory is the part of that window you write yourself. So it's the part you can shrink without losing information the task needs.
9444466e61:
There are also two things memory is not.

It isn't auto memory. That's a separate feature in which Claude writes its own notes to ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/. It loads the first 200 lines or 25 KB of a MEMORY.md index at the start of each session and reads topic files on demand. CLAUDE.md is what you write for the team. Auto memory is what Claude writes for itself, machine-local and not shared.

And memory isn't the system prompt. If you need an instruction at that level for scripted runs, the docs point to --append-system-prompt at launch.

Companion example 01_memory_is_text.py assembles the first request from the fixture repo. It prints what loads at launch, what loads on demand, and the estimated token cost of each.
81b7fe62d9: The docs list the locations in load order, from broadest scope to most specific, so a project instruction appears in context after a user instruction. Read the table below for three columns at once: where the file lives, who receives it, and whether it travels through version control. The exam item is almost always about the third column.
a9c4fc2951:
The user row carries the first sentence of the official knowledge bullet: user-level settings apply only to that user and are not shared through version control.

The classic symptom is "Claude follows our error-handling convention for me and not for my new teammate". The classic cause is that the convention went into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, perhaps months ago, perhaps by asking Claude to remember it.

The fix is to move the convention into a committed project file and delete it from the personal one, so there's one source of truth. Asking the teammate to copy your file is wrong on every axis. It's manual. It drifts the moment either file changes. And it mixes your personal preferences into their setup.
47384e364c:
Two rows deserve a second look.

Local. Some earlier material, including the previous draft of this guide, described CLAUDE.local.md as deprecated. The current memory page documents it as a supported file. It loads alongside CLAUDE.md and is appended after it within each directory, and you should add it to .gitignore. The docs also describe its one weakness. If you use several git worktrees, a gitignored file exists only in the worktree where you created it. For personal instructions across worktrees, import a file from your home directory instead (@~/.claude/my-project-instructions.md).

Managed policy. Individual settings can't exclude this file. That makes it the right home for organization-wide guidance and the wrong home for a hard guarantee, because it is still memory. Section 16 returns to this.
1c0e6ddd3b:
The hierarchy also includes things that aren't named "CLAUDE.md".

  • User-level rules in ~/.claude/rules/ load before project rules.
  • An AGENTS.md is read when the repository has no CLAUDE.md in the working directory or above (the default setting is claude-md-or-agents-md). A repository that wants one file for several tools can write @AGENTS.md as the first line of a CLAUDE.md, with Claude-specific instructions after it.
  • Directories added with --add-dir don't contribute memory unless the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD is set to 1.
  • The additionalDirectories setting never loads CLAUDE.md or rules. It only grants file access.
3b26ef33b1:
From here on, everything uses one repository. The rules only become clear when you can see which file loads for which task.

It's a telecom order platform: two Spring Boot services with a saga between them, a shared library, a React storefront with tests next to the components, and Flyway migrations in each service. It lives in the companion folder as fixtures/order-platform/, so you can reproduce every claim in the following sections.
f5a58416d0:
The other four rule files follow the same pattern and are in the companion folder. Notice two design choices before moving on.

First, the Kafka standard is imported from the orders directory file, not from the root. Only work on the saga needs it, so a session fixing CSS never pays for it.

Second, web/src/cart/Cart.test.tsx matches both react-components.md and react-tests.md on purpose. Component conventions are useful context when you write a component test.

The paths syntax has no exclusion form you should rely on (check the docs). So design globs to include what you mean and nothing else.
87989f3b1b:
This section is the reference for the rest of the chapter. It states what the docs say, in the order Claude Code does it, and marks what the docs leave open.

Where a step is a simplification, the companion simulator memsim.py implements that simplification so you can run it. The simulator is a teaching tool, not Claude Code's code. In a real session, /context shows what loaded at launch, and an InstructionsLoaded hook (section 15) logs every later load with its reason.
9173dd94a6: User. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, plus ~/.claude/rules/*.md files that have no paths. User rules load before project rules, so a project rule appears later in context. Neither overrides the other.
d7e322e835: Ancestors of the working directory. Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md from the directory where you started and from every directory above it. Content runs from the filesystem root down to the working directory, so the file closest to where you launched is read last. Within a directory, CLAUDE.local.md comes after CLAUDE.md. (The project can also use .claude/CLAUDE.md at the same level as ./CLAUDE.md.)
de09ecd4fb: Unscoped rules. Files in .claude/rules/ without paths frontmatter load at launch "with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md". The docs don't say where they land among a directory's files. The simulator places them after the project root's own files (check the docs).
c1619aff21: Exclusions. A claudeMdExcludes setting removes files whose absolute path matches a glob. It can live at user, project, local or managed scope, and the arrays merge across scopes. Managed policy files can't be excluded.
5c99a4b999:
Claude also discovers CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files in subdirectories below the working directory. It doesn't load them at launch.

When does it load them? The two relevant docs pages disagree. The memory page says Claude Code includes them "when Claude uses the Read, Write, or Edit tool on a file in those subdirectories". The configuration-debugging page says "when Claude reads a file in that directory with the Read tool, not at launch and not when writing or creating files there". Since they disagree about writes, treat Read as the safe trigger and check the docs for Write and Edit.

If Claude already used one of those tools on the subdirectory's CLAUDE.md itself, it isn't loaded a second time. A short message such as Loaded services/orders/CLAUDE.md appears in the terminal.
828de284cc:
Rules with paths work the same way. They trigger "when Claude uses the Read, Write, or Edit tool on a file matching the pattern, not on every tool use". The match also works when Claude reaches the file through a symlinked path to the project directory. Imports inside a lazily loaded file load with it (the Kafka standard arrives with services/orders/CLAUDE.md).

Two things the docs don't say. First, whether every directory between the working directory and a deeply nested file contributes its CLAUDE.md, or only the file's own directory. The simulator loads each directory on the way down, shallowest first (check the docs). Second, whether @imports are expanded inside rule files. The simulator doesn't expand them, and the chapter's own rules don't use them.
b6a624fcbc: The core of memsim.py is short enough to read. The launch phase builds the chain from the ceiling down to the working directory. The touch phase handles nested files and path rules:
df0f7b581c:
A Java developer will recognise the shape. It's classpath-style discovery in two phases: an eager scan at startup and a lazy resolution on first use, like Spring's component scan against @Lazy beans.

The analogy has one useful implication. Eager work has a startup cost that everyone pays. Lazy work has a first-touch cost paid by whoever needs it. The design question is always which side an instruction belongs on.

java/MemSim.java in the companion folder is a single-file Java port of the same two phases (ancestors, unscoped rules, imports, nested files, glob matching). Run it with java MemSim.java on JDK 17 or later.
4ee1359749: Companion example 03_simulator_scenarios.py runs the repo with a managed file, a user file for Maria, and the approved external import. It prints the sets below. Token counts are the simulator's estimates (characters divided by four).
3eb78ab09d:
The fourth row shows why the starting directory is a design variable. The docs' monorepo guide makes the same point. Start at the repository root, and only the root file loads; subdirectory files load on demand. Start in a subdirectory, and that directory's file plus every ancestor's loads at launch.

Teams with a clear module ownership model often tell people to start Claude in the module they're working on. That gives the module's memory from the first message and keeps the other modules' memory out entirely. Teams whose tasks cross modules start at the root and accept lazy loading.
8060d37a61: Size. A CLAUDE.md of up to 4 MiB loads in full; a larger file is skipped. The recommendation is under 200 lines per file. Over that, Claude Code shows a warning at startup and in /status. A second warning appears when files that are each within the limit add up past a combined limit (the number isn't given; check the docs). Each CLAUDE.md, rules file and @path import counts as a separate file.
6b4e7aad83: Subagents. The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md to keep their context smaller. A custom subagent loads it just as the main conversation does, unless its definition sets omitClaudeMd. Critical instructions for a custom subagent belong in the agent file's body, which is its system prompt.
57f9490f56: Instructions that compete. Claude Code adds its own guidance about commits and pull requests. If your memory sets different rules, the docs point to the includeGitInstructions and attribution settings, so your text doesn't argue with the built-in text.
cbabb50c5b: Safe mode. claude --safe-mode starts with all customizations disabled, including CLAUDE.md. If the problem disappears there, a customization is the cause. Managed policy still applies.
fd4d964ac9:
A CLAUDE.md can pull other files into itself with @path/to/file. Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch, alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them.

The syntax is the Markdown you'd write anyway. See @README for project overview and @package.json for available npm commands imports both files, wherever the @ appears in the line.

Spring has had an equivalent since Boot 2.4: spring.config.import, which lets one configuration file name others to merge in. Maven's <parent> and Gradle's apply from: are older cousins. The idea is the same. Keep each file about one thing, and compose them.
8aecf10736:
Here are the rules, all from the memory page except where marked.

  • Paths. Relative paths resolve relative to the file that contains the import, not the working directory. Absolute paths and home paths (@~/.claude/my-notes.md) are allowed.
  • Depth. Imported files can import others, up to a maximum depth of four hops.
  • Spaces. A path with spaces needs a backslash before each space. Without it, the path ends at the first space. A path wrapped in quotes isn't imported at all.
  • Code. Import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks. That's how you mention @README without importing it: put it in backticks.
  • External imports. An import in a project-level memory file is "external" when its path resolves outside the working directory, as the home-directory import above does. The first time Claude Code meets external imports in a project, it shows an approval dialog listing the files. If you decline, they stay disabled and the dialog doesn't appear again. User-scope files such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are trusted and load their imports without the dialog.
ad8041d7e3:
One sentence in the docs decides how you use imports: imports "help you organize a long file but don't reduce its context cost, because imported files also load at launch".

An import isn't a link the model can choose to follow. It's a transclusion. A root file that imports ten standards puts the same ten standards in context as a root file that contains them.

That's what the exam means by "selectively":

  • Import into the root only what applies to nearly every task (here, the error format and the Git workflow).
  • Import module-specific material from that module's own CLAUDE.md. The Kafka standard comes from services/orders/CLAUDE.md, so it loads lazily.
  • Move file-type conventions into path-scoped rules. These do reduce the cost, because they don't load until a matching file is touched.
82b23a3f2f:
Imports are also the sanctioned way to keep personal additions out of a shared file. The root CLAUDE.md in the fixture ends with @~/.claude/order-platform-local.md. On Maria's machine the file exists. Once she approves external imports, her sandbox URL is in context. On Ravi's machine the file doesn't exist, and the import is skipped without breaking anything.

The same mechanism serves a repository that maintains an AGENTS.md for several tools. Its CLAUDE.md can start with @AGENTS.md and add Claude-specific lines below. The docs mention the symlink alternative (ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md) and its Windows caveat: git checks a committed symlink out as a text file unless core.symlinks is enabled.
c537048cd1: Example 08_claude_md_linter.py finds the import mistakes that happen in practice. Run it on the fixtures and you get these three, each with its cause:
9da0d62cf6:
The first is the relative-path trap. The author thought in terms of the repository root; the loader resolves from the importing file. The Spring parallel is a classpath: resource name versus a file: path, and a Java developer won't make that mistake twice.

The second is the depth limit, which fails silently. The chain looks right in the editor, and the fifth file just isn't in context.

The third is real. The 592-line fixture mentions Playwright tags such as @smoke and @full outside backticks, and the loader treats them as import attempts. (What happens to an unresolvable target isn't documented; check the docs.) Wrap annotations, decorators, tags and handles in backticks everywhere in memory files. It costs two characters.
f1235d6583:
The docs are direct on this point: "All discovered files are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other."

The ordering is deterministic. Managed comes first, then user, then project files from the filesystem root down to the working directory, with CLAUDE.local.md after CLAUDE.md in each directory. The docs add that "instructions closer to where you launched Claude are read last".

What the docs don't promise is that the last instruction wins. On conflicts they say: "if two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily". And on user versus project rules: "Neither set overrides the other: if a user rule and a project rule conflict, Claude may follow either one, so keep the two consistent."
e4eddb64b0:
In practice a model leans toward later and more specific text. That's why many teams believe directory files "override" the root. The belief mistakes a tendency for a rule.

A tendency fails under exactly the conditions where you need the rule:

  • a long context, where the later instruction sits far from the work;
  • an instruction phrased more weakly than the earlier one;
  • a contradiction between two files, neither of which is closer to the task.

Example 11_conflict_and_order.py builds a small tree with an indentation conflict across four files and an injection-style conflict across two. It prints the order in which the five files enter the context. Then it runs a crude detector that groups instructions by topic and reports differing values, and shows the repair:
b7b0d8b4f7:
The repair isn't "make the later one stronger". State the general rule together with its exception, in the file that owns the exception. The root says "indent with 2 spaces everywhere except services/billing". The billing file says "indent with 4 spaces in this module only". Now there's nothing for the model to reconcile.

The same repair works for personal preferences that disagree with the team's. Say a user file says "answer tersely" and a project file requires long explanations in commit messages. They don't conflict if the project file says commit messages. If a personal preference really must override a project convention, the honest fix is to change the convention.

Rule files that contradict the root are the commonest cause of drift after a split. The periodic review the docs recommend catches them, and /doctor prompt-audit (Claude Code v2.1.283 or later) can do that review for you. It looks for instructions written for older models, references to files or commands that no longer exist, and files that contradict each other. It changes nothing until you ask.
fd175b213f:
Everything so far says big files cost more. This section puts numbers on it, using the estimator in example 07_token_estimator.py.

The estimator is deliberately crude. It divides the character count by four, a rough figure for English prose and Markdown that tends to undercount code, identifiers and punctuation-heavy tables. It's reliable for ratios between two layouts of the same content, which is what a split decision needs. It's unreliable for an invoice.

For exact counts, the Messages API has a token-counting endpoint (client.messages.count_tokens; check the docs for the current signature). The example calls it when run with --live and an API key.
e2a0638f60:
First, the fixtures. The worked repo's memory files are small. The root CLAUDE.md is about 200 tokens, the largest rule (java-services.md) about 130, and a directory file about 110. The always-loaded part comes to roughly 560 tokens: the root file, its imports, the unscoped security rule, a short managed file and one user file. A task that touches Java adds the orders file, one import and one rule, about 300 more. This is the size the docs' advice produces.

Now the counter-example: the bloated file from section 11, 592 lines generated by fixtures/monolith/gen_monolith.py. It's 36,673 characters, about 9,170 tokens, and it loads at launch for every task, including the README typo. Against the split layout that section builds, the measured cost per task type is:
b510bd7a67:
The per-request cost is only the first number. Memory is part of the input of every request in a session. So a 25-request session with the monolith sends about 229,000 input tokens of memory. The split layout averages about 56,000.

Prompt caching changes the price of repeating a prefix. Suppose the cache reads at a tenth of the base input price (check the docs for current multipliers and the cache lifetime). Then the same two figures become roughly 31,000 and 7,700 token-equivalents.

Caching cuts the bill. It doesn't remove the other two costs. The tokens still occupy the context window, and the model still has to find the three lines about migrations among nine hundred. The docs name the adherence problem directly: "Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence."
0e5d8a812b:
Two cost traps are specific to this design.

Path rules load again after compaction. A rule that loads on demand sits in message history. Compaction summarises it, and it has to load again the next time its trigger fires. So a very large path-scoped rule, edited repeatedly in a compacting session, pays repeatedly.

Overlap multiplies. A test file that matches three rules loads all three. The fixture's React test loads the component rule and the test rule on purpose. But a careless set of broad globs (**/* in two rules) quietly turns scoped rules back into always-on ones.
3d372ec4ff:
Placement decides whether the text reaches the model. Wording decides whether the model acts on it.

The docs give a short rule for wording: write instructions concrete enough to verify. "Use 2-space indentation", not "Format code properly". "Run npm test before committing", not "Test your changes". "API handlers live in src/api/handlers/", not "Keep files organized".

A useful self-test: could a reviewer look at a diff and say, without judgement, whether the instruction was followed? "Constructor injection only; no @Autowired on fields" passes. "Write clean code" doesn't, and it costs the same tokens.
e999d0bac0:
The second rule is about what to leave out. The docs say to keep CLAUDE.md to facts Claude should hold in every session: build commands, conventions, project layout, "always do X" rules. If an entry is a multi-step procedure, or only matters for one part of the codebase, move it to a Skill or a path-scoped rule.

The /doctor checkup applies the same logic to a checked-in file. It proposes cutting content Claude can derive from the codebase, such as directory layouts, dependency lists and architecture overviews. It keeps pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from tool defaults.

The reasoning is economic. Claude can read build.gradle.kts and list the dependencies itself, at the moment it needs them. Pasting them into memory pays for them on every request, and it guarantees they go stale. What Claude can't derive is the part worth the tokens: why the team does something unusual, what looks like a good idea and isn't, which command must be run from which directory.
96d406ac65:
The other failure is a file that grows because every thought gets recorded. The docs offer four triggers that guard against it. Add a line when:

  • Claude makes the same mistake a second time;
  • a code review catches something Claude should have known about this codebase;
  • you type the same correction into chat that you typed last session;
  • a new teammate would need the same context to be productive.

One correction is an event. The second occurrence is a convention. The exception is a hard requirement that must hold the first time. That's a candidate for a hook or a permission, not a line of memory.
c122293886: Here is the same content written twice. The left version is typical of a file that has grown by accretion. The right version is what the checklist produces. Both are real excerpts from the fixtures; the bad one comes from fixtures/broken_repo/CLAUDE.md, which the linter flags line by line.
76ec3b703f:
What changed, line by line?

  • The vague sentences became verifiable commands.
  • The shouting disappeared. The linter counts emphasis words, because a file where eight things are IMPORTANT has none that is.
  • The two "never" lines moved out of prose into a deny rule, and the good version says so. That also tells the reader (and the model) why it can't do it.
  • The directory tree went, because Claude can list a directory.
  • The wrong convention (@Autowired on fields, unquoted, so also a mistaken import) was replaced by the right one, with the reason attached.

A model that knows the reason can apply it to a case you didn't list.
ed0913af0c:
Three smaller habits help.

Group under headers and bullets. The docs say organised sections are easier for Claude to follow than dense paragraphs. One instruction per bullet, so a later edit can change one thing. Date or ticket the temporary. "Field injection is allowed only under batch/ until ORD-881 closes" tells a reviewer when to delete the line.

Models change too. The docs advise revisiting memory after major model releases. An instruction that worked around an older model's limitation may be pure overhead for a newer one. They also suggest reviewing CLAUDE.md changes in pull requests, like documentation. A Stop hook is an option for proposing updates while the gap is fresh.
07c58891c9:
/init analyses the codebase and generates a starting CLAUDE.md with build commands, test instructions and the conventions it discovers. If a file already exists, it suggests improvements instead of overwriting.

Set CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1 before running it, and it becomes an interactive multi-phase flow. It asks which artifacts to set up (CLAUDE.md files, skills, hooks) and presents a proposal before writing. It also reads other tools' rule files (Cursor rules, Copilot instructions) and, with the variable set, AGENTS.md.

Treat the output as a draft. It infers, and a wrong inferred convention becomes team memory the moment it's committed.

/doctor proposes trims for a checked-in file. /doctor prompt-audit checks all instruction files for staleness and contradiction.

Older Claude Code versions had a quick-add shortcut for appending a line to memory. The current memory page doesn't describe it. To add to a file, ask Claude ("add this to the project CLAUDE.md") or edit it from /memory.
6ddaea3bce:
Task statement 3.1 names the skill: splitting a large CLAUDE.md into focused topic-specific files in .claude/rules/.

The procedure below is the one the companion example applies to a real 592-line file, and its output is checked. After the split, every content line of the original appears exactly once in the new layout. The estimated cost at launch drops from about 9,170 tokens to about 1,370.
29d589fdfb:
The fixture is the file a team ends up with after two years of "add it to CLAUDE.md". It has 26 sections. By line count the largest are the Java conventions (42), the architecture map (34), the React conventions (35), the alert catalogue (33) and the Java testing conventions (33).

About a third of it is reference material that no coding task needs at launch: the endpoint, topic and alert catalogues, the ADR index, the environment variable table, the glossary, and the first-week checklist.
b11c2cdb8c: Tag every section by audience. For each one, ask: who needs this, and when? There are five answers: every task, one language or framework, one folder or module, one kind of file that appears in many folders, and a procedure run occasionally. A sixth answer exists, and it's the most common: nobody, during coding.
d5c1cfdbfd: Every task stays in the root file or in a short imported file: commands, a summary of the architecture, the non-negotiable rules. The docs recommend under 200 lines. In practice, aim for under 60.
85c183b53d: One module becomes either a directory CLAUDE.md or a rule with a folder glob. Prefer the directory file when the module is self-contained and its owners should maintain the file next to the code. Prefer the rule when the same instructions apply to scattered paths.
381a69bb46: Reference material moves to docs/, with a one-line pointer in the root ("details in docs/architecture.md, read it when you need it"). Generated catalogues are deleted from memory, because the generator is the source.
1009f6c9f3: Check what you moved. Run the linter, and run the simulator for three representative files. Then start a real session and compare /context with the prediction. Section 15 describes the verification loop.
7d0516801a: Here is the split plan as a table. It's the real data structure in 09_split_600_line.py, abridged to one row per destination. The reasoning in the last column is what you'd write in the pull request description.
1613267073: The generated root file is 41 lines. In a real project you'd also trim the commands to the ten used weekly. But the point is the shape: commands, a three-line architecture summary with a pointer, three always-rules, two imports, and a closing line that tells the reader where the rest lives.
0665abb4df:
The exercise carries two cautions.

First, java-services.md is still 88 lines and 1,531 tokens, because three sections share an audience. That meets the docs' 200-line guidance. But if the rule grows, split it again, perhaps into persistence and logging rules with narrower globs. Splitting isn't a one-time event.

Second, every rule that has paths is a bet that nobody needs it before a matching file is touched. That bet is right for "Spring service conventions" and wrong for "no PII in logs", which is why the security rule stays unscoped.

When in doubt, ask what happens if the session is compacted, or if the instruction is needed in the first prompt before any file has been opened. A rule that must be present then can't be path-scoped.
468882e0bf:
A path-specific rule is a Markdown file in .claude/rules/ whose YAML frontmatter has a paths field of glob patterns. The docs sum these conditional rules up: they "only apply when Claude is working with files matching the specified patterns".

Section 06 set out when they load. This section is about when to choose them and how they compare with the alternatives. That's the question the exam asks.
d0861e4eb2:
Here's the scenario in the exam guide. A codebase has several areas: frontend components, backend services, shared libraries. Test files sit next to the code they test throughout the tree. So a test for Cart.tsx is Cart.test.tsx in the same folder, and there are dozens of such folders. The team wants test conventions applied consistently wherever a test is written. Which approach?

The exam's options are some mixture of these:

  • a CLAUDE.md file in every directory that has tests;
  • one rule file with a glob such as **/*.test.tsx;
  • the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md;
  • a Skill.

The answer is the rule file with a glob pattern. The reason has three parts, and you should be able to state them without notes.
1ff14e1625:
The boundary is a kind of file, not a place. A directory CLAUDE.md scopes by location. Test files are scattered across every location, so the directory approach needs a copy in each. Sixty copies of the same text drift.

A directory file over-matches. Even if you accepted the copies, a directory CLAUDE.md loads when Claude touches any file in the subtree. Editing Cart.tsx would also load the test conventions: wrong scope, extra tokens.

The alternatives load at the wrong time. The root file loads for every task, including ones that never touch a test. That's the cost problem of section 09. A Skill loads when the task matches its description. That's a judgement made from the prompt, not a guarantee tied to the file being edited. The path rule is the only mechanism whose trigger is the file itself.

Example 16_exam_scenarios.py tests the claim. It builds sixty feature folders with colocated tests. It shows that the path rule loads for all sixty tests and for nothing else. It shows that the root-file option loads the conventions into an unrelated billing task. And it shows that sixty directory files also load when you edit a component.
194131fcaf:
The docs' monorepo guide gives the decision in two lines. Use a per-directory file when "directory owners maintain their own conventions" and instructions should be "versioned with the code". Use a path-scoped rule when "you want all conventions in one place, or the same rule applies to many scattered paths".

There's a third lever for the same problem. The docs mention that skills also accept a paths frontmatter field with glob patterns, so they load automatically only when Claude works with matching files. This suits a skill that lives at the repository root but applies only to certain files, such as a migration skill scoped to **/migrations/**. That's a Skill-shaped procedure with a path-shaped trigger. The rule is still the right home for passive conventions that every edit of that file type should respect.
44e61af105: Frontmatter. paths is the only field Claude Code reads from a rule. Any other field is ignored without an error, and that includes a typo such as path:. The frontmatter is removed before the rule enters context. paths accepts a YAML list or a comma-separated string. If the YAML between the markers doesn't parse, the frontmatter is ignored and the rule loads as if it had no paths. claude --debug shows the parse error.
c70a0ef7f3: Discovery. All .md files under .claude/rules/ are found recursively, so subfolders like frontend/ and backend/ work. Symlinks are supported, and circular ones are handled. A symlink whose target is outside the working directory is treated like an external import: it needs approval, and after approval only rules without paths load. Shared rules in ~/.claude/rules/ need no approval and apply to every project on the machine.
175744087d: Persistence. The rule sits in message history, so compaction summarises it. For a rule that must persist, the docs advise dropping the paths frontmatter or moving it to the project-root CLAUDE.md. Example 15 demonstrates this.
2d41564a2d: Nested rule directories. The docs refer to rules in nested .claude/rules/ directories loading on demand. The memory page doesn't say how a paths glob in such a file is anchored: to the project root, or to its own directory. Check the docs before relying on it.
29566b751e:
The glob is where path rules go wrong in practice. It's also where the exam can ask a pointed question: which pattern matches which file?

The docs show a handful of patterns and their meaning, and don't name the glob library. That leaves three sets of behaviour: ones the docs state, ones that follow the common convention and that you should verify, and ones that differ between libraries.

The chapter separates them, and the tests in example 05_glob_tests.py carry the same split. A DOC_FACTS table holds behaviours stated in the docs. A CONVENTIONS table holds assumptions marked "check the docs".
2c669e9a5f:
The third row decides most exam questions. In a gitignore file, *.md without a slash matches Markdown files at any depth. In a paths list, it matches only the project root.

If you wrote the patterns thinking in gitignore terms, you have the wrong mental model. The symptom is a rule that never loads for files in subfolders. The portable habit: start any pattern that should match at any depth with **/.
099a32dbaa:
Python's standard library has a trap of its own. fnmatch is the glob matcher many people reach for, and its * matches any characters, including /. So fnmatch("docs/guide.md", "*.md") is true, the opposite of the docs' table. And ** has no special meaning, so fnmatch("Cart.test.tsx", "**/*.test.tsx") is false, because the pattern demands a slash.

Example 04_glob_matchers_matrix.py runs eighteen cases through three implementations in globlib.py:

  • fnmatch;
  • a gitignore-style matcher, where no slash in the pattern means match at any depth;
  • a glob-star matcher, where * stays within a path segment, ** spans segments, **/ may match zero directories, and braces expand.

Five of the eighteen cases differ, and they're the five worth memorising:
4a1dc858b7:
Three more behaviours follow from the glob-star model.

** as a whole segment matches any number of directories, including none. So web/**/*.test.tsx matches web/Cart.test.tsx and web/src/a/b/Cart.test.tsx. A ** embedded inside a name (foo**bar) isn't a recursion operator in most libraries, so don't write it.

A single * never crosses a slash. That's why services/*/src/main/java/**/*.java matches services/orders/src/main/java/... but not services/orders/api/src/main/java/.... The pattern names exactly one directory between services and src. If your modules nest, say so with services/**/src/main/java/**/*.java.

Brace expansion multiplies. The docs give src/*.{ts,tsx} as two patterns and {a,b}/{c,d}/*.{ts,tsx} as eight. They also bound the cost. One rule's whole paths list shares a budget of 1,000 expanded patterns and 4 MiB. Patterns without braces don't count. A pattern that would exceed the budget is used unexpanded, so its literal braces match no files.

The test suite checks all three: two and eight patterns, the 40 by 40 fallback, and 5,000 brace-free patterns costing nothing against the budget.
56a3cafdeb:
Some things the docs don't state. Confirm them on your version before depending on them:

  • whether a leading ./ or / is accepted (the examples never use one, and the linter warns);
  • whether ** matches dot-directories such as .github/ (many glob libraries skip them by default);
  • whether matching is case-sensitive on macOS and Windows;
  • how Windows path separators are treated;
  • what library is behind it.

So the safe style is the one the docs' examples use: paths relative to the project root, forward slashes, no leading dot, and a short list of explicit patterns.
4ff62615e8: The second source of path-rule bugs is YAML, not globs. In YAML, a plain (unquoted) scalar can't start with certain indicator characters. * is one of them: it begins an alias. So this frontmatter doesn't say what it appears to say:
c8fba18174:
A YAML parser reports "while scanning an alias" for the first form. And here the docs' rule bites. When the YAML doesn't parse, Claude Code ignores the frontmatter and loads the rule as if it had no paths.

So the bug isn't "the rule never loads". It's "the rule loads in every session, for every task". There's no failure to see in the output. The only symptoms are a larger /context, and a rule appearing in the Memory files list at launch where it should be absent.

Example 06_yaml_quoting_trap.py tries ten frontmatter shapes:

  • the quoted list;
  • the single-quoted list;
  • the inline list;
  • the comma-separated string, including the brace case, "src/**/*.{ts,tsx}, lib/**/*.ts". That one must be split on commas outside braces. Whether Claude Code does that isn't stated, so prefer a list;
  • an unquoted pattern starting with * (unscoped);
  • a key typo (unscoped, silently);
  • an unquoted pattern starting with a letter (fine);
  • a file with no frontmatter at all.

One habit prevents the whole class. Always quote globs. Then run claude --debug once and check that the rule appears only after a matching file is touched.
1a4e6856b8:
A team new to Claude Code tends to put every kind of guidance in CLAUDE.md, because it's the one file everyone has heard of.

The mechanisms below differ on two axes that matter. The first is when the content enters the context: always, on a file trigger, on a task trigger, on a user command, or never. The second is whether the harness enforces it.

Memory, rules and Skills are all guidance. They shape the model's behaviour and prevent nothing. Permissions and hooks are enforcement. The harness applies them in code, whatever the model decides.
a86392f53b:
The docs make the memory/enforcement distinction in so many places that it's clearly meant to be tested. One example: "Claude treats [CLAUDE.md and auto memory] as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead." And in the managed-policy discussion: "Settings rules are enforced by the client regardless of what Claude decides to do. CLAUDE.md instructions shape Claude's behavior but are not a hard enforcement layer."

So when a scenario says "despite the CLAUDE.md instruction, Claude once ran the production migration", the answer that adds stronger wording ("NEVER, under any circumstances") is the distractor. The answer is a deny permission or a hook. Optionally, keep the same sentence in memory, so the model knows why it will be blocked and doesn't keep trying.
ff9cba050d:
The docs add a caution about Bash deny rules. They match the literal command string, not the underlying executable. So Bash(rm *) doesn't stop /bin/rm or find -delete. For a hard guarantee, use a PreToolUse hook or the sandbox. Treat a deny list as a speed bump for the common path, and a hook as the guarantee.

Chapter 03 covers hooks. The point for this chapter is only that deciding where an instruction lives starts with the question below.
9288e1c336:
The skill the exam names is diagnosing hierarchy problems, such as a teammate not receiving instructions that live in a user-level file, and using /memory to verify which memory files are loaded.

Before the cases, here's a precise statement of the tools. The docs split jobs that the exam wording treats as one.

/memory lists the CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and other memory file locations across user and project scopes, including ones that don't exist yet. It lets you open any of them in your editor, and it toggles auto memory.

/context shows everything occupying the window, by category. Its "Memory files" list shows which CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files loaded at launch. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files don't appear there, because they load on demand. When one loads, a Loaded line with its path appears in the terminal.

In the exam, when the question offers /memory as the verification tool, that's the intended answer, and it's the one the task statement names. In daily work, use both: /memory to see and edit, /context to see what's actually in the window.
e3c5a087d6:
Maria says Claude always routes errors through the global handler for her. Ravi, who joined Monday, reports that Claude hand-builds error bodies in his controllers. Same repo, same prompt.

The diagnosis follows the loop in the figure below. Example 12_diagnose_teammate.py performs it on the fixtures. It prints each person's launch set, then searches the loaded text for the rule:
5f4b98457c: Fix it by moving the rule into docs/standards/api-errors.md, which the root imports, and commit it. Delete it from Maria's user file so there's one source of truth. Don't ask Ravi to copy her file.
3fa2b62a12:
Tests written in web/src/cart/ follow the team conventions. Tests in the new web/src/plans/ use fireEvent and stub fetch.

The cause: the conventions live in web/src/cart/CLAUDE.md, a directory file created for the first feature, and plans/ has no copy. The fix is the official sample's fix. Delete the directory file and create .claude/rules/react-tests.md with paths on web/**/*.test.tsx.

To verify, open a new session and ask Claude to edit web/src/plans/Plan.test.tsx. Then look for the Loaded line, or check /context. By design, a rule scoped by paths won't be in the launch list. So checking /context before the file is touched proves the opposite of what people expect.
23c8a19043:
Two inverse reports share the same diagnostic.

"The JUnit rule appears in /context at launch even though it has paths." The frontmatter didn't parse (usually an unquoted glob), so the rule is unscoped. See section 13.

"The services/billing/CLAUDE.md doesn't appear in /context." That's correct: subdirectory files load on demand. Ask Claude to read a file under services/billing, and a Loaded line appears.

The docs add a practical tip for testing a new directory file. Create it from your shell, not by asking Claude to write it. A file Claude has already used a tool on counts as already in the conversation, so the subtree mechanism won't load it again.
692112f779:
Sometimes /context and the terminal messages aren't enough. Maybe you need to know why a rule loaded twice, or why a nested file never appeared in a long session. For that there's an InstructionsLoaded hook.

It fires when a CLAUDE.md or rules file loads into context: at session start for eagerly loaded files, and again for lazy loads. Its fields are file_path, memory_type (User, Project, Local, Managed), load_reason (session_start, nested_traversal, path_glob_match, include, compact), globs, trigger_file_path and parent_file_path. The matcher runs against load_reason, so "path_glob_match|nested_traversal" logs only lazy loads.

The hook can't block anything, and its exit code is ignored. It exists for observability. The companion folder has a real hook command, instructions_loaded_logger.py, and example 13 replays a simulated session through it. The timeline it produces is the one in FIG 5:
1f513ce87e:
One more family of causes belongs here, because people routinely misdiagnose it as a memory problem.

The built-in Explore and Plan subagents skip CLAUDE.md. A delegated search doesn't know your conventions unless the delegating prompt restates them. A custom subagent loads it, unless its definition sets omitClaudeMd.

And a long session that was compacted may have lost an instruction. It might have existed only in conversation, in a nested file that hasn't reloaded, or in a path rule that hasn't matched since (docs). The remedy for the first case is to write it into CLAUDE.md.
8a0d27568c:
For an organization of several hundred engineers, the question is how to get a baseline in front of everyone without relying on every repository to copy it. The mechanism is the managed policy file.

The first design decision is to separate two things the docs keep apart. Guidance (code style, quality guidelines, data-handling reminders, behavioural instructions) belongs in the managed CLAUDE.md. Enforcement (blocked tools, commands and file paths, sandbox isolation, environment variables, login restrictions) belongs in managed settings.

Example 14_managed_rollout.py builds both artifacts and checks the properties that matter.
7ec1edd38a:
Delivery is whatever your fleet already uses: MDM, Group Policy, Ansible or similar. The managed-settings page lists several delivery mechanisms for settings: server-managed from the claude.ai console, MDM or OS-level policy, a file in the system directory, and settings supplied by an embedding host. When more than one reaches a machine, Claude Code by default uses one and ignores the others. (The page explains the order, and the opt-in to apply all.)

If a managed settings file exists but can't be parsed, Claude Code refuses to start. That's why the example validates the JSON before shipping.

A team that prefers one artifact can carry the guidance inline in the managed settings, in a claudeMd key. It's honoured only in managed and policy settings; setting it in user, project or local settings has no effect. Precedence is the same as the file: it loads before user and project CLAUDE.md. Its scope is every Claude Code session on the machine, in every repository. So repository-specific guidance still belongs in the repository.
63be058861:
Two properties make the managed file different from the others, and the example tests both.

It can't be excluded. The user's claudeMdExcludes can remove their own user file and any project file by glob, but the managed file stays. The example lists three matching patterns and shows managed: loaded | user: excluded.

And it isn't enforcement. A managed CLAUDE.md that says "never paste customer data" shapes behaviour, and it's the right place to say it. But the control that blocks reading a secrets directory is the managed deny rule.

The settings precedence list puts managed settings first, then the command line, then local, project and user, with arrays merging across scopes. /status shows the active setting sources and whether managed settings are in effect.
38c6c77eaf: Pilot on a handful of machines. Place both files. Run /status (the managed source appears in the setting sources line) and /context (the managed CLAUDE.md is listed). Check that a prohibited action is actually denied, not merely discouraged.
8ab5e141df: Roll out with your fleet tool, and run a compliance probe that compares the file's hash with the shipped hash. Example 14 returns OK, DRIFT or MISSING per machine. The files are root-owned system files, so local edits are drift to correct, not a feature.
1eadf9fc5e: Make the repositories consistent. Publish a template repository with the short root file, the standard rule set, and a .claude/settings.json with the team deny list. Add a CODEOWNERS entry for CLAUDE.md, .claude/ and docs/standards/, so changes to memory get the same review as changes to code. The docs advise treating CLAUDE.md edits like any documentation change.
10a31d3f44: Lint in CI. Run the linter from example 08 on each repository. It exits non-zero on errors such as a broken import or an unparsed rule frontmatter, and it warns on size. For very large estates, the docs suggest moving shared conventions out of per-directory files into plugins distributed through an internal marketplace, so one team owns them centrally.
0c5a6736a9: Handle monorepos. People working in one team's package shouldn't pay for another team's memory. Start Claude from the package directory. Or set claudeMdExcludes for packages they never touch. It works at user, project, local or managed scope. Patterns are matched against absolute paths, so begin relative-style patterns with **/.
26d51e8596:
The Java parallel for this whole section is a company parent POM with the Maven Enforcer plugin. The parent POM sets dependency and plugin management for every module. That's guidance, in the sense that a child can still declare what it likes. The Enforcer fails the build on banned dependencies. That's enforcement.

Teams that confuse the two end up with a parent POM full of conventions that nothing checks. A managed CLAUDE.md without a managed deny list looks exactly like that.

Spring Cloud Config offers a second parallel. A central config server supplies defaults per application and profile, local files add the rest, and the precedence order says who wins. The difference from both is, again, the resolver. Here the central policy doesn't win. It just comes first.
2a6a4eca67: Each row of the table has a version that fails and a version that works. The codes after the table show the first six as you'd meet them.
792c0976c7:
The exam presents a scenario with four options. For 3.1 and 3.3, the wrong options are usually plausible engineering ideas that fix the wrong layer. They reword the text, copy the file, put it somewhere that loads too often or too rarely, or rely on memory for something it can't enforce.

Work through each scenario before reading the reasoning. The companion example 16_exam_scenarios.py verifies the first five by experiment.
3b48395497:
The symptom is a per-person difference in the same repository. That points at scope, not wording or timing. User-level memory is personal and not in version control.

A restart reloads what's on their disk, and the instruction isn't on their disk (A). Louder wording changes nothing about who receives the text (C). Copying her file (D) is manual, it drifts, and it imports her unrelated personal preferences. It's the answer that sounds practical and is wrong.

Verification: each person's /memory and /context lists differ in exactly one file. Example 12 does this.
a49b070d8b:
The conventions apply to a kind of file spread across places. A path-scoped rule is scoped by pattern, exists once, and loads only when a matching file is touched.

The root file (A) loads for every task, including a billing change that never touches a test. Directory files (B) multiply the text and drift. They also load when a non-test file in the same folder is edited. A Skill (D) loads on a judgement about the task, not on the file being edited. So the conventions might be missing exactly when a test is written.

Example 16 measures A, B and C on sixty colocated test folders.
d900b9221e:
Adherence falls with length and with conflicting or irrelevant content, and the cost is paid on every request. B cuts launch memory and loads the rest by file pattern or invocation.

A adds emphasis to a file that's already too long. C moves the same text into five files that all load at launch; the docs say imports "don't reduce [the] context cost". D moves the problem to the one scope teammates can't see.

Example 09 splits a 592-line file with the same recipe: about 9,170 tokens at launch become about 1,370.
9334f71291:
The docs say that if the YAML between the markers doesn't parse, Claude Code ignores the frontmatter and loads the rule as if it had no paths.

A is false: rules with paths load on a matching file. C invents a size rule. D confuses globs with regular expressions.

The diagnostic is that a scoped rule should not be in the launch list. claude --debug shows the parse error. Example 06 shows ten frontmatter shapes and the scope each produces.
ddac099cc0:
Here the boundary is a place and an owner. That's what a directory CLAUDE.md is for. It sits next to the code, loads on first touch of the subtree, and the owning team maintains it. The docs' monorepo guidance says per-directory files fit when "directory owners maintain their own conventions" and when instructions should be "versioned with the code".

B, with a match-everything glob, is the root file again. C loads the payments text for every task. D is the user-scope bug of scenario 1.

The trap in this scenario is reaching for the 3.3 answer by reflex. Read whether the question is about a place or about a kind of file.
4a79a9c706:
Memory is context, not enforced configuration. The docs say so repeatedly. They direct anything that must hold to a PreToolUse hook or permissions, which the client applies whatever the model decides.

A and B repeat the same unenforced text. D loads it only when a migration file is touched, which isn't when a shell command is typed.

Note that Bash deny rules match command strings, not executables. So a hook is the stronger guarantee (docs).
153d217a1e:
Ancestors of the working directory load at launch; subdirectories load lazily. Starting in services/billing makes the directory file part of the launch set. That's a deliberate choice for teams that work module by module.

A and D contradict the documented hierarchy. C confuses directory files with rule files; paths is a rule field.

A test tip from the docs: create the file from your shell, then ask Claude to read a file in that directory.
23d323c0f2:
Relative paths resolve relative to the file containing the import, not the working directory (docs).

A is false: imports work in any CLAUDE.md, and the fixture's orders file uses one. C invents a constraint. D is the opposite of the docs: "A path wrapped in quotes isn't imported at all."

The linter in example 08 reports this exact mistake, with the hint that the file exists relative to the repo root.

af612d65e4:
Done when:

  • you can state the load order without notes;
  • you've seen an unquoted glob silently unscope a rule, and you know the one-line check for it;
  • you can split a long file into root, imports, path rules and Skills, and defend each placement;
  • the linter's three import findings make sense from the rules in section 07;
  • you can explain in three sentences why a managed CLAUDE.md isn't a security control.
